title: Supreme Court: Senior citizen discount can't be combined with promos
summary: In a statement on Wednesday, October 14, the High Court reversed lower-court rulings that found Orville Ong guilty of violating Republic Act (R.A.) No. 7432, as amended by Republic Act No. 9994 or…

blocks.text: The logo of the Supreme Court at the Supreme Court Building in Manila.

MANILA, Philippines — The Supreme Court has acquitted a Bacolod City hotel general manager charged with violating the Senior Citizens Act, ruling that statutory elderly discounts cannot be combined with existing promotional or group-negotiated rates.

In a statement on Wednesday, October 14, the high court reversed lower court rulings that found Orville Ong guilty of violating Republic Act No. 7432, as amended by Republic Act No. 9994, or the Expanded Senior Citizens Act of 2010.
Ong was charged after hotel guests, lawyer Paul S. Alcazaren, 66, and Eric Gadiana, 70, were denied an additional 20% senior citizen discount on their room accommodations.
Ong contended that the hotel had already extended a 20% discount on the room rates negotiated for members of the Cebu Bikers Club, to which both guests belonged.
Although the deduction was integrated into the total lump sum rather than itemized separately on the official receipt, Ong argued that the discount had already been fully applied.

While the Municipal Trial Court in Cities, the Regional Trial Court, and the Court of Appeals had all previously sustained Ong's conviction, the Supreme Court ruled in his favor, clarifying that the hotel was under no obligation to grant a second 20% markdown.
Clarifying the framework governing senior citizens' benefits, the Supreme Court emphasized that senior citizen discounts cannot be stacked on top of other promotional offers.

Under existing regulations, when goods or services are offered at promotional or discounted rates, senior citizens can choose either the promotional rate or the statutory 20% senior citizen discount, whichever yields greater savings.
However, businesses are not mandated to enforce both simultaneously.
"Granting an additional discount beyond what the law allows would unfairly benefit the customer at the business’s expense," the Court noted in a press statement released Wednesday.
The Supreme Court stressed that statutory privileges must be enforced with fairness toward commercial establishments.

“The State’s pursuit of public welfare cannot be allowed to impose undue or confiscatory burdens on private establishments, whose continued viability is essential to the long-term effectiveness of the law,” the high court declared.

The ruling sets a precedent for hospitality, food and retail service providers nationwide, confirming that businesses fulfilling mandatory discount percentages through negotiated group rates or sales promotions are protected against claims of non-compliance under RA 9994.
